fixes.explanation: Yes, baker! The passage closes with "…He will have compassion on His afflicted ones." (Isaiah 49:13). Compassion also showed up in verse 10, where the One who has compassion on them leads them beside springs of water. That's a gentle place to land.

Not anger, friend. The verse says, "For the LORD has comforted His people, and He will have compassion on His afflicted ones." (Isaiah 49:13). The afflicted ones get compassion. That's the reason given for the mountains to break forth in song.

Contempt isn't in this verse, baker. The verse says, "For the LORD has comforted His people, and He will have compassion on His afflicted ones." (Isaiah 49:13). The afflicted ones get compassion from the LORD. That's where this passage lands.

Babylon never gets named in this call, baker. The Servant says, "Listen to Me, O islands; pay attention, O distant peoples…" (Isaiah 49:1). Kings do show up later, in verse 7, when they see Him and rise. The call itself names islands and distant peoples, and that's a big mailing list.

Close to a campsite, but no tent here, friend. The text says, "He made Me like a polished arrow; He hid Me in His quiver." (Isaiah 49:2). A quiver is what holds arrows, so that's where this one is tucked away. A tent is for campers, not arrows.

No tower in this verse, baker. The Servant says, "He made Me like a polished arrow; He hid Me in His quiver." (Isaiah 49:2). The quiver is the case that holds the arrows, and this arrow is tucked away close in it.

No king in this line, baker. The Servant says, "yet My vindication is with the LORD, and My reward is with My God." (Isaiah 49:4). Right after saying "I have labored in vain," He puts His reward with God.

That's it, baker! The Servant says, "…for I am honored in the sight of the LORD, and My God is My strength…" (Isaiah 49:5). Just before this, He said He had spent His strength (Isaiah 49:4). Honored in the LORD's sight AND God is His strength. That's a good place to stand.

Not a stranger, friend. The Servant says the LORD formed Him from the womb to be His Servant (Isaiah 49:5). He also says, "…I am honored in the sight of the LORD…" That's the picture the Servant gives, and it's nothing like a stranger's.

That role isn't named in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth." (Isaiah 49:6). Here the LORD names a light for the nations. Jerusalem doesn't come up in this verse.

Standing back isn't in this verse, baker. The LORD says, "Kings will see You and rise, and princes will bow down…" (Isaiah 49:7). The kings rise, and the princes bow down. That's a big turn for the One who was despised and abhorred by the nation.

That's it, baker! The Servant is appointed "to say to the prisoners, 'Come out'" (Isaiah 49:9). Two little words for the prisoners. I know a thing or two about waiting in a dark drawer, so I like those words a LOT.
Opposite direction, friend. The Servant is appointed "to say to the prisoners, 'Come out'" (Isaiah 49:9). I think anybody sitting in the dark would much rather hear "Come out" than "Stay put."

No patience speech here, baker. The Servant is appointed "to say to the prisoners, 'Come out'" (Isaiah 49:9). It's a short word, and it's about leaving. I bet a prisoner would take that over a long speech.

You got it, baker! "For He who has compassion on them will guide them and lead them beside springs of water." (Isaiah 49:10). The guide is the One who has compassion on them. A walk beside springs of water sounds like a pretty good way to travel.

That's right, baker! The LORD says, "Behold, they will come from far away, from the north and from the west, and from the land of Aswan." (Isaiah 49:12). People are on the way, coming from the north, the west and Aswan. A full house is on its way.

No storm in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "Behold, they will come from far away, from the north and from the west, and from the land of Aswan." (Isaiah 49:12). He says "Behold," and what comes into view is people, not weather.

No army and no Babylon here, baker. The LORD says, "Behold, they will come from far away, from the north and from the west, and from the land of Aswan." (Isaiah 49:12). It's a crowd of people coming, from the north, the west and Aswan.

That's right, baker! The text says, "Shout for joy, O heavens; rejoice, O earth; break forth in song, O mountains! For the LORD has comforted His people…" (Isaiah 49:13). The reason is right there after the "For." The LORD has comforted His people, and the heavens, the earth and the mountains each get a call to celebrate.
